evidence: src/infrastructure/http/BadRequestError.ts: class BadRequestError extends Error, documented as raised when an HTTP request is malformed before it reaches a use case.

src/infrastructure/http/RequestReader.ts: optionalString and requiredString throw BadRequestError and never write responses; requiredString reuses optionalString, so the type check is written only once.

src/infrastructure/http/middleware/errorHandler.ts: STATUS_BY_KIND is the only place that maps DomainErrorKind to HTTP status, and errorHandler handles DomainError, BadRequestError, malformed JSON and the 500 fallback all in one function.
src/infrastructure/http/createApp.ts: createApp sets up the express.json body parser, the routes, the 404 fallback and errorHandler, which all belong to the same HTTP adapter concern.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
The unit passes. All four files deal with one concern: the Express HTTP adapter. createApp.ts builds the app. RequestReader.ts parses request bodies and reports bad input with BadRequestError. BadRequestError.ts defines that HTTP-level error. middleware/errorHandler.ts turns errors into HTTP responses.

The module uses its own abstractions consistently. RequestReader.ts reports every parse failure through BadRequestError and never writes a response itself. errorHandler.ts is the only file that maps errors to status codes. Each rule lives in one place: requiredString builds on optionalString instead of repeating the type check, and the domain-error-to-status mapping exists only in STATUS_BY_KIND. Two status codes are written outside that table: 400 for BadRequestError and the request-body parse failure, and the 404 'Route not found' fallback in createApp.ts. Each covers a different case, so they don't copy a rule that should live in one place. Nothing goes around the module's own abstractions.
